To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the retention of 15NO3 in soil organic matter is rapid and dynamic, and that the relative strength of the SOM retention mechanism varies with soil properties and forest age.

1) the SOM sink for 15N in mineral soil is a dynamic, not static, process; 2) the SOM sink is active in mineral soils of all ages, not just in mature or old growth forests; and 3) SOM N remains subject, at least over the long term, to active cycling and potentially loss from the soil to stream water.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the retention of nitrate N in mineral soil organic matter ( SOM) in different forest age classes.
understanding the role of soil organic matter as an important sink and source of nitrogen in forest ecosystems.
the role of soil organic matter in the retention of nitrate nitrogen (N) in mineral soils of forests receiving elevated atmospheric deposition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SOM N retention in forest ecosystems is an important process, but the relative importance of this sink in controlling NO3 N losses from ecosystems is poorly constrained.

the retention of NO3 in mineral soil organic matter is an important process in forest ecosystems that can be influenced by the C/N ratio of the SOM, but that the retention process is short term and may not be sufficient to explain the long term low stream NO3 concentrations observed at the Hubbard Brook Ecosystem Study.
the SOM pool in the mineral soil is a significant and dynamic N sink that may help to explain why mature forest watersheds receiving elevated N deposition do not experience NO3 N loss.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the retention of NO3 in soil organic matter is not a static process but a dynamic one.
the SOM pool is a dynamic and potentially important sink for NO3 in the short term.
SOM N is a dynamic, but important, sink for NO3 in forests.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SOM N can provide a significant sink for N in forest soils, and this sink may be especially important during periods of high N deposition and in forests approaching or in effective N saturation.
SOM N retention is a dynamic process that can occur across a range of forest ages.
SOM can be an important N sink in mineral soil in forests of all age classes, but that SOM is not a permanent sink and remains subject to active N cycling and potentially loss to the stream.
